A '''theograph''' (or '''theoplot'''<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Varady | first1=Andras B. | last2=Wood | first2=Richard M. | title=Improving uptake of population health management through scalable analysis of linked electronic health data | journal=Health Informatics Journal | date=2024 | volume=30 | issue=3 | article-number=14604582241259344 | doi=10.1177/14604582241259344 | pmid=39095387 | doi-access=free }}</ref>) is a type of graph to visualise patient journeys.<ref>{{cite web | title=A 10-year story: visualising patient journeys | website=Nuffield Trust | date=2019-03-18 | url=https://www.nuffieldtrust.org.uk/resource/a-10-year-story-visualising-patient-journeys | access-date=2025-07-25}}</ref><ref name=heu>{{Cite web | url=https://healtheconomicsunit.nhs.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/Theograph-how-to-guide.pdf | title=Theographs - A 'how to' guide | website=healtheconomicsunit.nhs.uk}}</ref> It has also been used in education.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://sure.sunderland.ac.uk/id/eprint/12858/|title=The use of theographs to understand the journeys of children excluded from school|first=Martin-Denham|last=Sarah|date=November 10, 2020|website=sure.sunderland.ac.uk}}</ref>

==Structure==
Theographs are a type of longitudinal history or health and care event timeline in a graphical form. They show the contacts an individual has with different services over time. Time is shown on x-axis, while different symbols represent different types of contact on the y-axis.<ref name=heu />
